Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Visual Attention Exploration in Vision-Based Mamba Models
papers.research_question: How do attention patterns in vision-based Mamba models vary across blocks and stages, and how are they influenced by the order in which image patches are arranged into sequences?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a visual analytics tool for exploring attention patterns in vision-based Mamba models and uses it to investigate the impact of different patch-ordering strategies on learned attention.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduced a visual analytics tool for exploring attention patterns in VMamba blocks, finding that blocks within the same stage have distinct patterns, patch order significantly influences patterns, and patches close in the input sequence have similar patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Blocks within the same stage exhibit significantly different attention patterns.
Some blocks exhibit complementary attention patterns, enabling the model to selectively focus on different image regions.
Attention patterns show a hierarchy: early stages exhibit strong spatial correlation, while later stages become more content-dependent.
The order in which patches are arranged into sequences significantly influences the resulting attention patterns.
Patches that are close in the input sequence generally exhibit similar attention patterns.
papers.limitation: The current tool focuses on content-agnostic attention patterns by averaging over many images, and does not provide content-relevant attention patterns for specific images.
future_direction: Explore more complex VMamba models with additional stages and blocks per stage.
Integrate additional views into the tool to present content-relevant attention patterns for diagnosing specific images.
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) have emerged as an efficient alternative to transformer-based models, offering linear complexity that scales better than transformers. One of the latest advances in SSMs, Mamba, introduces a selective scan mechanism that assigns trainable weights to input tokens, effectively mimicking the attention mechanism. Mamba has also been successfully extended to the vision domain by decomposing 2D images into smaller patches and arranging them as 1D sequences. However, it remains unclear how these patches interact with (or attend to) each other in relation to their original 2D spatial location. Additionally, the order used to arrange the patches into a sequence also significantly impacts their attention distribution. To better understand the attention between patches and explore the attention patterns, we introduce a visual analytics tool specifically designed for vision-based Mamba models. This tool enables a deeper understanding of how attention is distributed across patches in different Mamba blocks and how it evolves throughout a Mamba model. Using the tool, we also investigate the impact of different patch-ordering strategies on the learned attention, offering further insights into the model's behavior.

papers.title: Emergence of Primacy and Recency Effect in Mamba: A Mechanistic Point of View
papers.research_question: How do primacy and recency effects emerge in the Mamba architecture, and what are the underlying mechanisms for long-term and short-term memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three mechanisms underlying primacy and recency effects in Mamba: sparse channels for long-term memory, exponential decay for short-term memory, and delta modulation by input regularity.
papers.conclusion: Mamba exhibits primacy and recency effects due to sparse long-term memory channels, short-term decay dynamics, and input-sensitive gating, challenging the necessity of attention for structured memory.
papers.key_findings:
Primacy effect is supported by a sparse subset of channels in the selective SSM block that persistently encode early tokens.
Recency effect arises from exponential decay in the recurrence, giving more weight to recent inputs.
Adding distractor tokens reduces recency accuracy, showing short-term memory limits.
Memory allocation is modulated by semantic regularity: repeated relations increase forgetting of intermediate items.
The discretization parameter Δt adapts to input frequency, with higher Δt for lower-frequency inputs leading to faster forgetting.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled synthetic recall task, which may not generalize to complex natural language tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader settings and downstream applications
Decoupling the gating factor Δt from input injection to improve memory dynamics
papers.abstract: We study memory in state-space language models using primacy and recency effects as behavioral tools to uncover how information is retained and forgotten over time. Applying structured recall tasks to the Mamba architecture, we observe a consistent U-shaped accuracy profile, indicating strong performance at the beginning and end of input sequences. We identify three mechanisms that give rise to this pattern. First, long-term memory is supported by a sparse subset of channels within the model's selective state space block, which persistently encode early input tokens and are causally linked to primacy effects. Second, short-term memory is governed by delta-modulated recurrence: recent inputs receive more weight due to exponential decay, but this recency advantage collapses when distractor items are introduced, revealing a clear limit to memory depth. Third, we find that memory allocation is dynamically modulated by semantic regularity: repeated relations in the input sequence shift the delta gating behavior, increasing the tendency to forget intermediate items. We validate these findings via targeted ablations and input perturbations on two large-scale Mamba-based language models: one with 1.4B and another with 7B parameters.

papers.title: JoMA: Demystifying Multilayer Transformers via JOint Dynamics of MLP and Attention
papers.research_question: How does the joint training dynamics of MLP and attention in Transformers lead to effective learning, and why does the attention pattern (first sparse then dense) emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the JoMA framework, a mathematical analysis that characterizes the joint training dynamics of MLP and attention layers in Transformers, showing that attention first becomes sparse then dense, which helps learn hierarchical concepts.
papers.conclusion: JoMA provides a framework for understanding the joint training dynamics of MLP and attention, revealing how self-attentions at different layers interact to learn latent feature hierarchies.
papers.key_findings:
JoMA predicts that with nonlinear activations, attention first becomes sparse to learn salient tokens, then becomes dense to learn less salient tokens.
With linear activation, attention becomes sparse over time, consistent with prior work.
JoMA qualitatively explains how tokens combine to form hierarchies in multilayer Transformers when input tokens are generated by a latent hierarchical generative model.
Experiments on models trained from Wikitext2/Wikitext103 and pre-trained models (OPT, Pythia) verify the theoretical findings.
The framework overcomes limitations of prior analyses by incorporating residual connections and MLP nonlinearity.
papers.limitation:
The orthogonality assumption of embedding vectors may not hold exactly in real-world Transformers.
Training of embedding vectors is not considered in the analysis.
Self-attention is parameterized independently, not through embedding matrices, which may affect generalization.
future_direction: Analyzing the case when embedding vectors are not orthogonal (due to Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma).
Incorporating training of embedding vectors into the dynamics.
Generalizing self-attention parameterization to use embedding matrices.
papers.abstract: We propose Joint MLP/Attention (JoMA) dynamics, a novel mathematical framework to understand the training procedure of multilayer Transformer architectures. This is achieved by integrating out the self-attention layer in Transformers, producing a modified dynamics of MLP layers only. JoMA removes unrealistic assumptions in previous analysis (e.g., lack of residual connection) and predicts that the attention first becomes sparse (to learn salient tokens), then dense (to learn less salient tokens) in the presence of nonlinear activations, while in the linear case, it is consistent with existing works that show attention becomes sparse over time. We leverage JoMA to qualitatively explains how tokens are combined to form hierarchies in multilayer Transformers, when the input tokens are generated by a latent hierarchical generative model. Experiments on models trained from real-world dataset (Wikitext2/Wikitext103) and various pre-trained models (OPT, Pythia) verify our theoretical findings. Code can be found in https://github.com/facebookresearch/luckmatters/tree/yuandong3.

papers.title: LaTIM: Measuring Latent Token-to-Token Interactions in Mamba Models
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained, token-level interpretability for Mamba state space models (SSMs) to understand their selective sequence processing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATIM, a novel token-level decomposition method for Mamba-1 and Mamba-2 that enables fine-grained interpretability by reformulating SSM computations to reveal token-to-token interaction patterns.
papers.conclusion: LATIM significantly improves interpretability for Mamba models, providing clearer insights into their selective processing mechanisms and opening new directions for improving their reliability and effectiveness in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
LATIM provides clearer insights into Mamba's selective processing mechanisms compared to existing interpretability methods like Mamba-Attention and MambaLRP.
LATIM achieves better faithfulness scores (AUC, AP, R@K) in the copying task and lower Alignment Error Rate (AER) in machine translation.
Analysis with LATIM reveals that Mamba's recall limitations in long-context tasks may stem from its sparse and decaying focus on relevant tokens.
An exact version of LATIM, achieved by removing non-linearities (SiLU), yields zero decomposition error while maintaining task performance.
LATIM's token-level heatmaps more accurately capture expected interaction patterns (e.g., diagonal copying) and translation alignments than baseline methods.
papers.limitation:
LATIM relies on an approximation strategy to decompose token contributions due to the non-linearity introduced by the SiLU activation; an exact decomposition requires model modifications and re-training.
Evaluation focuses primarily on tasks like Copying and Machine Translation where token interactions are well understood; assessing interpretability quality in more complex tasks like Retrieval-based Generation is harder and may require further validation.
future_direction: Further validation of interpretability quality in complex tasks with human evaluations.
Extending LATIM to other state space models or linear recurrent architectures, which may require adapted decomposition techniques.
Investigating the impact of token-level interpretability on improving model robustness and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs), such as Mamba, have emerged as an efficient alternative to transformers for long-context sequence modeling. However, despite their growing adoption, SSMs lack the interpretability tools that have been crucial for understanding and improving attention-based architectures. While recent efforts provide insights into Mamba's internal mechanisms, they do not explicitly decompose token-wise contributions, leaving gaps in understanding how Mamba selectively processes sequences across layers. In this work, we introduce LaTIM, a novel token-level decomposition method for both Mamba-1 and Mamba-2 that enables fine-grained interpretability. We extensively evaluate our method across diverse tasks, including machine translation, copying, and retrieval-based generation, demonstrating its effectiveness in revealing Mamba's token-to-token interaction patterns.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Rethinking Attention: Exploring Shallow Feed-Forward Neural Networks as an Alternative to Attention Layers in Transformers (Student Abstract)
papers.research_question: Can shallow feed-forward networks effectively mimic and replace attention mechanisms in Transformers for sequence-to-sequence tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow feed-forward networks can effectively replace attention layers in Transformers for translation tasks, rivaling original performance, highlighting their adaptability and potential for streamlining architectures.
papers.conclusion: Empirical evidence shows that 'attentionless Transformers' can achieve comparable performance to original Transformers, indicating attention is not strictly necessary, but current optimization methods require knowledge distillation for training.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder self-attention replacement methods achieve competitive BLEU scores compared to the baseline Transformer.
ALR is the most effective approach for encoder replacement, with high performance and small parameters.
Full Transformer replacement with ALR works well for decoder self-attention but performs worse for cross-attention.
Replacement approaches increase parameter count and reduce flexibility in handling variable sequence lengths.
ELR performs the worst due to simplicity discarding helpful encoder structures.
papers.limitation:
Replacement approaches have more parameters than the original attention layers.
Fixed-size feed-forward networks lack flexibility in handling sequences of different lengths.
Current optimization methods cannot train these attentionless Transformers from scratch without knowledge distillation.
future_direction: Further optimization of feed-forward network hyperparameters using advanced parameter search like Bayesian optimization.
Enabling smaller feed-forward networks for replacement to reduce parameter bottleneck.
papers.abstract: This work presents an analysis of the effectiveness of using standard shallow feed-forward networks to mimic the behavior of the attention mechanism in the original Transformer model, a state-of-the-art architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. We substitute key elements of the attention mechanism in the Transformer with simple feed-forward networks, trained using the original components via knowledge distillation. Our experiments, conducted on the IWSLT2017 dataset, reveal the capacity of these ”attentionless Transformers” to rival the performance of the original architecture. Through rigorous ablation studies, and experimenting with various replacement network types and sizes, we offer insights that support the viability of our approach. This not only sheds light on the adaptability of shallow feed-forward networks in emulating attention mechanisms but also underscores their potential to streamline complex architectures for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

papers.title: Towards Universality: Studying Mechanistic Similarity Across Language Model Architectures
papers.research_question: Does mechanistic understanding transfer across different model architectures? Specifically, how similar are the features and circuits in Transformer and Mamba models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer and Mamba models learn similar interpretable features as extracted by Sparse Autoencoders, and their induction circuits are structurally analogous, with a nuanced Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that SAE feature similarity is a useful measure for cross-architectural universality, revealing significant similarity between Transformer and Mamba features and circuits, with an Off-by-One motif in Mamba.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE features in Pythia and Mamba are similar, with high Max Pairwise Pearson Correlation (MPPC).
Feature similarity is affected by semantic complexity; simpler features have higher correlation.
Induction circuits in Mamba are analogous to those in Transformers, but with an Off-by-One motif where information is written into the SSM state at the next token.
SAE features show depth specialization across architectures, with matched features appearing at proportionally similar layers.
The neuron baseline shows almost zero similarity, indicating SAEs are better for cross-architecture comparison than neuron-based methods.
papers.limitation:
SAEs may not capture all true features and might capture combinations of features rather than the features themselves.
Circuit universality analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative automated comparison tools.
future_direction: Automating circuit discovery and comparison for quantitative measurement of circuit universality.
Further study on the Off-by-One motif in Mamba circuits to understand its purpose and formation.
papers.abstract: The hypothesis of Universality in interpretability suggests that different neural networks may converge to implement similar algorithms on similar tasks. In this work, we investigate two mainstream architectures for language modeling, namely Transformers and Mambas, to explore the extent of their mechanistic similarity. We propose to use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to isolate interpretable features from these models and show that most features are similar in these two models. We also validate the correlation between feature similarity and Universality. We then delve into the circuit-level analysis of Mamba models and find that the induction circuits in Mamba are structurally analogous to those in Transformers. We also identify a nuanced difference we call \emph{Off-by-One motif}: The information of one token is written into the SSM state in its next position. Whilst interaction between tokens in Transformers does not exhibit such trend.

papers.title: Trained Mamba Emulates Online Gradient Descent in In-Context Linear Regression
papers.research_question: How does Mamba perform in-context learning for linear regression tasks, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical analysis showing that Mamba can be trained to perform in-context linear regression by emulating online gradient descent, with exponential convergence and a loss bound comparable to Transformers.
papers.conclusion: Mamba effectively performs in-context linear regression through a mechanism akin to online gradient descent, with theoretical guarantees and experimental validation.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba performs in-context linear regression by updating its hidden state in a manner that emulates online gradient descent.
The training dynamics converge exponentially to the in-context learning solution.
The population loss bound is O(1/N), matching the sample complexity of Transformers for linear regression ICL.
The ICL mechanism in Mamba is distinct from Transformers, as it relies on sequential state updates rather than global attention.
The selection mechanism in Mamba is crucial for ICL, enabling task adaptation, unlike static S4 models.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis relies on specific assumptions, including A=-I, fixed w∆, Gaussian initialization of WB and WC, large hidden dimension dh, and small learning rate.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, emerge as an efficient Transformer alternative with linear complexity for long-sequence modeling. Recent empirical works demonstrate Mamba's in-context learning (ICL) capabilities competitive with Transformers, a critical capacity for large foundation models. However, theoretical understanding of Mamba's ICL remains limited, restricting deeper insights into its underlying mechanisms. Even fundamental tasks such as linear regression ICL, widely studied as a standard theoretical benchmark for Transformers, have not been thoroughly analyzed in the context of Mamba. To address this gap, we study the training dynamics of Mamba on the linear regression ICL task. By developing novel techniques tackling non-convex optimization with gradient descent related to Mamba's structure, we establish an exponential convergence rate to ICL solution, and derive a loss bound that is comparable to Transformer's. Importantly, our results reveal that Mamba can perform a variant of \textit{online gradient descent} to learn the latent function in context. This mechanism is different from that of Transformer, which is typically understood to achieve ICL through gradient descent emulation. The theoretical results are verified by experimental simulation.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning Beyond Transformers: An Investigation of State Space and Hybrid Architectures
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work internally in state-space and hybrid architectures, and how do these mechanisms compare to transformers across different task types?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends the analysis of function vectors (FVs) to state-space and hybrid architectures, revealing that while models can exhibit similar ICL performance, their internal mechanisms differ, with FVs being more critical for parametric knowledge retrieval than contextual understanding.
papers.conclusion: The work extends prior analysis of function vectors to diverse architectures and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of FVs across task types, while methodologically highlighting the importance of combining behavioral and mechanistic analyses.
papers.key_findings:
While LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internal mechanisms can remain different.
Function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers.
Mamba2 appears to use a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL.
FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval than for contextual knowledge understanding.
In hybrid models, ICL capabilities are primarily contributed by FVs located in self-attention layers, regardless of whether self-attention and SSM layers are stacked in parallel or sequentially.
papers.abstract: We perform in-depth evaluations of in-context learning (ICL) on state-of-the-art transformer, state-space, and hybrid large language models over two categories of knowledge-based ICL tasks. Using a combination of behavioral probing and intervention-based methods, we have discovered that, while LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internals could remain different. We discover that function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers, and speculate that Mamba2 uses a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL. FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval, but not for contextual knowledge understanding. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding across architectures and task types. Methodologically, our approach also highlights the importance of combining both behavioural and mechanistic analyses to investigate LLM capabilities.

papers.title: Demystify Mamba in Vision: A Linear Attention Perspective
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to Mamba's success and its significant superiority to linear attention Transformer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that Mamba is closely related to linear attention Transformer and identifies the forget gate and block design as key to its success. It then proposes MILA, a linear attention model that incorporates these designs and outperforms Mamba in vision tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals the close relationship between Mamba and linear attention Transformer, identifies the forget gate and block design as key to Mamba's success, and proposes MILA which surpasses vision Mamba models across multiple tasks while maintaining parallel computation and high inference speed.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba can be reformulated as a variant of linear attention Transformer with six major design distinctions: input gate, forget gate, shortcut, no attention normalization, single-head, and modified block design.
Empirical analysis shows the forget gate and block design are the core contributors to Mamba's superior performance.
The recurrent forget gate can be replaced by suitable positional encodings (e.g., LePE, CPE, RoPE) in vision tasks, preserving parallel computation and fast inference.
The proposed MILA model, incorporating the key designs, outperforms various vision Mamba models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.
MILA maintains parallelizable computation and achieves faster inference speed compared to recurrent Mamba models.
papers.limitation: There may be other small differences between the implementation details of Mamba and linear attention Transformer that are not exhaustive in this paper.
papers.abstract: Mamba is an effective state space model with linear computation complexity. It has recently shown impressive efficiency in dealing with high-resolution inputs across various vision tasks. In this paper, we reveal that the powerful Mamba model shares surprising similarities with linear attention Transformer, which typically underperform conventional Transformer in practice. By exploring the similarities and disparities between the effective Mamba and subpar linear attention Transformer, we provide comprehensive analyses to demystify the key factors behind Mamba's success. Specifically, we reformulate the selective state space model and linear attention within a unified formulation, rephrasing Mamba as a variant of linear attention Transformer with six major distinctions: input gate, forget gate, shortcut, no attention normalization, single-head, and modified block design. For each design, we meticulously analyze its pros and cons, and empirically evaluate its impact on model performance in vision tasks. Interestingly, the results highlight the forget gate and block design as the core contributors to Mamba's success, while the other four designs are less crucial. Based on these findings, we propose a Mamba-Inspired Linear Attention (MILA) model by incorporating the merits of these two key designs into linear attention. The resulting model outperforms various vision Mamba models in both image classification and high-resolution dense prediction tasks, while enjoying parallelizable computation and fast inference speed. Code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/MLLA.

papers.title: Rethinking Attention: Exploring Shallow Feed-Forward Neural Networks as an Alternative to Attention Layers in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can shallow feed-forward networks effectively mimic and replace attention mechanisms in Transformers for sequence-to-sequence tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow feed-forward networks can be trained via knowledge distillation to replace attention mechanisms in Transformers, achieving comparable performance on machine translation tasks.
papers.conclusion: Empirical evidence shows that Transformers do not necessarily require attention mechanisms, as shallow feed-forward networks can achieve similar performance when trained via knowledge distillation, though current optimization limitations prevent training from scratch.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow feed-forward networks can effectively replace attention layers in Transformers, with the Attention Layer Replacement (ALR) method being the most effective for encoder self-attention.
Decoder self-attention can be successfully replicated, but cross-attention replacement performs worse due to its complexity.
The replacement approaches increase parameter count and reduce flexibility in handling variable sequence lengths.
Knowledge distillation is necessary for training these attentionless Transformers, as current optimization methods cannot train them from scratch.
The viability of feed-forward networks as alternatives to attention mechanisms highlights potential for streamlining complex architectures.
papers.limitation:
Replacement approaches significantly increase the number of parameters.
The fixed-size feed-forward networks lack flexibility in handling sequences of varying lengths.
Cross-attention replacement performs worse due to the complexity of mapping between sequences.
future_direction: Optimizing hyperparameters of feed-forward networks using advanced parameter search like Bayesian optimization.
Training more complex feed-forward networks to better model the cross-attention module.
papers.abstract: This work presents an analysis of the effectiveness of using standard shallow feed-forward networks to mimic the behavior of the attention mechanism in the original Transformer model, a state-of-the-art architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. We substitute key elements of the attention mechanism in the Transformer with simple feed-forward networks, trained using the original components via knowledge distillation. Our experiments, conducted on the IWSLT2017 dataset, reveal the capacity of these "attentionless Transformers" to rival the performance of the original architecture. Through rigorous ablation studies, and experimenting with various replacement network types and sizes, we offer insights that support the viability of our approach. This not only sheds light on the adaptability of shallow feed-forward networks in emulating attention mechanisms but also underscores their potential to streamline complex architectures for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: RNN as Linear Transformer: A Closer Investigation into Representational Potentials of Visual Mamba Models
papers.research_question: How does Mamba's representational capacity compare to self-attention and linear attention in visual domains, and can we quantitatively evaluate feature maps to understand its long-range dependency modeling?
papers.core_contribution: This paper theoretically shows Mamba is a low-rank approximation of softmax attention, introduces a binary segmentation metric (Binary-AUC) for quantitative evaluation of activation maps, and demonstrates that self-supervised pretraining with DINO yields clearer activation maps and competitive performance for Vision Mamba.
papers.conclusion: Mamba balances efficiency and expressiveness, matching transformers in classification and outperforming linear attention in high-resolution segmentation and detection, while the Binary-AUC metric serves as a useful tool for model analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba can be viewed as a low-rank approximation of softmax attention, with higher representational capacity than linear attention but lower than softmax attention.
The proposed Binary-AUC metric quantitatively shows that self-attention produces the most discriminative feature maps, followed by Mamba, then linear attention.
Self-supervised pretraining with DINO yields clearer feature maps than supervised training.
Mamba achieves competitive linear probing accuracy on ImageNet (78.5%) and outperforms linear attention on downstream tasks requiring long-range dependencies.
Feature map quality (AUC) correlates with model performance and can be used to identify underperforming components (e.g., attention heads, register tokens).
future_direction: Improving the effectiveness of underperforming components (e.g., attention heads, register tokens) to further enhance the representational capacity of both attention and Mamba.
papers.abstract: Mamba has recently garnered attention as an effective backbone for vision tasks. However, its underlying mechanism in visual domains remains poorly understood. In this work, we systematically investigate Mamba's representational properties and make three primary contributions. First, we theoretically analyze Mamba's relationship to Softmax and Linear Attention, confirming that it can be viewed as a low-rank approximation of Softmax Attention and thereby bridging the representational gap between Softmax and Linear forms. Second, we introduce a novel binary segmentation metric for activation map evaluation, extending qualitative assessments to a quantitative measure that demonstrates Mamba's capacity to model long-range dependencies. Third, by leveraging DINO for self-supervised pretraining, we obtain clearer activation maps than those produced by standard supervised approaches, highlighting Mamba's potential for interpretability. Notably, our model also achieves a 78.5 percent linear probing accuracy on ImageNet, underscoring its strong performance. We hope this work can provide valuable insights for future investigations of Mamba-based vision architectures.

papers.title: Shaking Up VLMs: Comparing Transformers and Structured State Space Models for Vision & Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Investigates whether Mamba-based Visual Language Models (VLMs) are competitive alternatives to Transformer-based VLMs across multimodal tasks, particularly focusing on performance differences in coarse-grained tasks like captioning and fine-grained tasks like visual grounding.
papers.core_contribution: Mamba-based VLMs outperform Transformer-based VLMs in tasks like captioning and visual question answering but underperform in visual grounding, with the performance gap increasing with model scale. The study attributes this to Mamba's limitations in in-context multimodal retrieval tasks.
papers.conclusion: Mamba shows promising performance for tasks requiring image summarization but struggles with fine-grained retrieval tasks like visual grounding, indicating inherent limitations in retrieval-oriented tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba-VL variants match or surpass Pythia-VL in captioning, VQA, and reading comprehension tasks.
Pythia-VL consistently outperforms Mamba-VL in visual grounding tasks, and this gap widens with larger models.
Task-aware visual encoding provides minimal performance gains for Mamba-VL in grounding.
Transformers are more sample-efficient than Mamba in synthetic in-context multimodal retrieval tasks.
Increasing image resolution benefits both models, but Pythia-VL benefits more in grounding tasks.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to models up to 3B parameters.
future_direction: Exploring more efficient vision-language connectors for SSMs.
Further investigation into model hallucinations and improving reliability of VLMs.
papers.abstract: This study explores replacing Transformers in Visual Language Models (VLMs) with Mamba, a recent structured state space model (SSM) that demonstrates promising performance in sequence modeling. We test models up to 3B parameters under controlled conditions, showing that Mamba-based VLMs outperforms Transformers-based VLMs in captioning, question answering, and reading comprehension. However, we find that Transformers achieve greater performance in visual grounding and the performance gap widens with scale. We explore two hypotheses to explain this phenomenon: 1) the effect of task-agnostic visual encoding on the updates of the hidden states, and 2) the difficulty in performing visual grounding from the perspective of in-context multimodal retrieval. Our results indicate that a task-aware encoding yields minimal performance gains on grounding, however, Transformers significantly outperform Mamba at in-context multimodal retrieval. Overall, Mamba shows promising performance on tasks where the correct output relies on a summary of the image but struggles when retrieval of explicit information from the context is required.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Modularity in Transformers: Investigating Neuron Separability & Specialization
papers.research_question: How modular and task-specialized are neurons in transformer models? The paper investigates the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence for task-specific neuron clusters in transformers, showing that neuron importance patterns are partially present even in randomly initialized models and are refined by training.
papers.conclusion: The methods reveal interpretable modularity in transformers, and the overlap between random and trained models provides evidence for a weak Lottery Ticket Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific neuron clusters exist in transformers, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks.
Neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines.
MoEfication clusters correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models.
For ViT, classes with intuitive similarities (e.g., 'insects' and 'non-insect invertebrates') show higher overlap in selected neurons.
For Mistral, unlearning a text subset (e.g., 'PubMed Central') leads to performance drops in related MMLU subjects (e.g., 'professional medicine').
papers.limitation:
We focused on MLP neurons and did not analyze attention mechanisms, which play a crucial role in transformer models.
Our analysis was limited to a specific set of tasks and datasets, and may not generalize to all domains or model architectures.
The interpretation of neuron importance and specialization is still somewhat qualitative and could benefit from more rigorous statistical analysis.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to include attention mechanisms and their interaction with MLP layers.
Developing more sophisticated clustering techniques that can capture hierarchical relationships between neurons and tasks.
Investigating how neuron specialization evolves during the training process.
papers.abstract: Transformer models are increasingly prevalent in various applications, yet our understanding of their internal workings remains limited. This paper investigates the modularity and task specialization of neurons within transformer architectures, focusing on both vision (ViT) and language (Mistral 7B) models. Using a combination of selective pruning and MoEfication clustering techniques, we analyze the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets. Our findings reveal evidence of task-specific neuron clusters, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks. We observe that neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines. Additionally, we find that neuron clusters identified through MoEfication correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of transformer internals and offers insights into potential avenues for improving model interpretability and efficiency.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Characterizing Mamba's Selective Memory using Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: What types of tokens (e.g., parts of speech, named entities) and sequences (e.g., code, math problems) are more frequently forgotten by Mamba SSM language models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies specific token and sequence types (math-related tokens, organization entities, non-standard dialects) that Mamba language models are prone to forget, and links this selective memory to token frequency in pretraining data.
papers.conclusion: Mamba's memory is selective, with weaknesses in retaining math tokens, organization names, and non-standard dialects, motivating future research to improve retention of pertinent information.
papers.key_findings:
Mamba shows significantly higher information loss for math-related tokens (numbers, variables) and mentions of organization entities.
Reconstruction fidelity degrades more for African American Vernacular English (AAVE) compared to Standard American English (SAE) as sequence length increases.
Mamba exhibits a recency bias, forgetting earlier tokens more than recent ones.
Tokens with lower frequency in the pretraining data (e.g., numbers) tend to have higher omission rates.
Reconstruction performance declines sharply with increasing sequence length, especially for mathematical content.
papers.limitation:
Decoder errors could confound with information loss in Mamba's hidden states.
Only one SSM language model family (Mamba) is evaluated.
Only one linear recurrent architecture (SSM) is studied.
No solutions to the identified selective memory issues are provided.
No evaluation on downstream tasks is performed.
Potential distribution shift between Pile Uncopyrighted and the original Pile training dataset.
Lack of dialect taggers prevents full analysis of training corpus for non-standard dialects.
future_direction: Reconsider tokenization strategies (e.g., byte-level, digit-level) for SSMs.
Explore pretraining objectives tailored to SSM architectures, such as auxiliary reconstruction losses.
Develop methods to control Mamba's selective memory to better retain important information.
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) are a promising alternative to transformers for language modeling because they use fixed memory during inference. However, this fixed memory usage requires some information loss in the hidden state when processing long sequences. While prior work has studied the sequence length at which this information loss occurs, it does not characterize the types of information SSM language models (LMs) tend to forget. In this paper, we address this knowledge gap by identifying the types of tokens (e.g., parts of speech, named entities) and sequences (e.g., code, math problems) that are more frequently forgotten by SSM LMs. We achieve this by training an auto-encoder to reconstruct sequences from the SSM's hidden state, and measure information loss by comparing inputs with their reconstructions. We perform experiments using the Mamba family of SSM LMs (130M--1.4B) on sequences ranging from 4--256 tokens. Our results show significantly higher rates of information loss on math-related tokens (e.g., numbers, variables), mentions of organization entities, and alternative dialects to Standard American English. We then examine the frequency that these tokens appear in Mamba's pretraining data and find that less prevalent tokens tend to be the ones Mamba is most likely to forget. By identifying these patterns, our work provides clear direction for future research to develop methods that better control Mamba's ability to retain important information.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Controllability Analysis of State Space-based Language Model
papers.research_question: Can the Influence Score, a controllability measure derived from control theory, serve as a diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper validates the Influence Score, a novel controllability measure derived from Mamba's state-space parameters, as a diagnostic tool for SSM-based language models, revealing scaling effects, architectural signatures, and emergent behaviors related to model capacity and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The Influence Score is a promising diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models, revealing core architectural properties and emergent behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The Influence Score scales directly with model size and training data quality, serving as a proxy for model capacity.
Mamba exhibits consistent architectural signatures: a strong recency bias (position sensitivity) and a heavy concentration of influence in mid-to-late layers.
Emergent behaviors appear at scale: the largest model (mamba-2.8b-slimpj) intuitively ranks content words as more influential than function words and demonstrates robustness by decreasing internal influence when processing noisy inputs.
The Influence Score is largely insensitive to sampling temperature but increases systematically with prompt complexity.
The metric reveals a functional specialization across layers, with late layers showing significantly higher influence than early layers.
papers.limitation:
The Influence Score is an aggregated metric; future work should trace the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
The study was limited to three models; applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing to Transformers would be beneficial.
future_direction: Tracing the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
Applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing their influence fingerprints to traditional Transformers.
Using the Influence Score for guided generation, e.g., penalizing decoding paths that lead to unstable spikes in influence to improve model reliability.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have become powerful architectures for sequence modeling, yet their internal dynamics remain poorly understood compared to attention-based models. We introduce and validate the Influence Score, a controllability-based metric derived from the discretized state-space parameters of Mamba and computed through a backward recurrence analogous to system observability. The score quantifies how strongly a token at position k affects all later states and outputs. We evaluate this measure across three Mamba variants: mamba-130m, mamba-2.8b, and mamba-2.8b-slimpj, using six experiments that test its sensitivity to temperature, prompt complexity, token type, layer depth, token position, and input perturbations. The results show three main insights: (1) the Influence Score increases with model size and training data, reflecting model capacity; (2) Mamba exhibits consistent architectural patterns, including recency bias and concentrated influence in mid-to-late layers; and (3) emergent behaviors appear only at scale, with mamba-2.8b-slimpj uniquely prioritizing content words and reducing internal influence in the presence of noise. These findings establish the Influence Score as a practical diagnostic tool for interpreting and comparing SSM-based language models.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes. Such improvement is primarily attributable to their data specificity, not long-range dependency. On the other hand, ViTs suffer from non-convex losses. Large datasets and loss landscape smoothing methods alleviate this problem; (2) MSAs and Convs exhibit opposite behaviors. For example, MSAs are low-pass filters, but Convs are high-pass filters. Therefore, MSAs and Convs are complementary; (3) Multi-stage neural networks behave like a series connection of small individual models. In addition, MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction. Based on these insights, we propose AlterNet, a model in which Conv blocks at the end of a stage are replaced with MSA blocks. AlterNet outperforms CNNs not only in large data regimes but also in small data regimes. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

papers.title: MambaLRP: Explaining Selective State Space Sequence Models
papers.research_question: How to bring explainability, specifically Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), to the Mamba architecture to provide faithful explanations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MambaLRP, a novel Layer-wise Relevance Propagation method tailored for the Mamba architecture, which ensures the conservation property and provides faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: MambaLRP provides an efficient and faithful explanation method for Mamba models, enabling users to debug and build trust in these models through various use cases.
papers.key_findings:
MambaLRP adheres to the relevance conservation axiom, which is violated by a naive application of LRP to Mamba components like SiLU, selective SSM, and multiplicative gates.
MambaLRP outperforms various baseline explanation methods (e.g., Gradient × Input, Integrated Gradients, attention-based methods) in quantitative faithfulness evaluations across multiple models and datasets.
The method enables the uncovering of biases (e.g., gender bias in medical occupation classification) and the analysis of model capabilities (e.g., long-range dependency in needle-in-a-haystack tasks).
MambaLRP is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward and backward pass, comparable to Gradient × Input.
papers.limitation:
MambaLRP requires storing activations and gradients, leading to memory usage that depends on model architecture and input sequence length.
The method may be inapplicable when gradient information is inaccessible due to proprietary constraints.
future_direction: Explore the potential of MambaLRP across a broader range of applications and Mamba architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent sequence modeling approaches using selective state space sequence models, referred to as Mamba models, have seen a surge of interest. These models allow efficient processing of long sequences in linear time and are rapidly being adopted in a wide range of applications such as language modeling, demonstrating promising performance. To foster their reliable use in real-world scenarios, it is crucial to augment their transparency. Our work bridges this critical gap by bringing explainability, particularly Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), to the Mamba architecture. Guided by the axiom of relevance conservation, we identify specific components in the Mamba architecture, which cause unfaithful explanations. To remedy this issue, we propose MambaLRP, a novel algorithm within the LRP framework, which ensures a more stable and reliable relevance propagation through these components. Our proposed method is theoretically sound and excels in achieving state-of-the-art explanation performance across a diverse range of models and datasets. Moreover, MambaLRP facilitates a deeper inspection of Mamba architectures, uncovering various biases and evaluating their significance.
