papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Attention is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth
papers.research_question: What is the inductive bias of pure self-attention networks, and how do skip connections and MLPs counteract rank collapse in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that pure self-attention networks lose rank doubly exponentially with depth, converging to a rank-1 matrix, and that skip connections and MLPs are crucial in preventing this rank collapse.
papers.conclusion: This work exposes competing forces over rank collapse in self-attention networks, namely self-attention vs skip connections and MLPs, and develops a path decomposition method for analyzing SANs.
papers.key_findings:
Pure self-attention networks (without skip connections or MLPs) converge doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix.
Skip connections are crucial for mitigating rank collapse.
MLPs can slow down the convergence by increasing the Lipschitz constant.
Layer normalization does not mitigate rank collapse.
Transformers behave like ensembles of shallow networks due to skip connections.
papers.limitation: Removing skip connections for analysis introduces a drastic distribution shift in the MLP input, affecting observations.
future_direction: How to leverage the token-uniformity inductive bias to design more effective networks, perhaps better at utilizing long paths.
What are the practical implications for width-depth trade-off?
How to prove meaningful lower bounds of residue convergence for transformers?
papers.abstract: Attention-based architectures have become ubiquitous in machine learning, yet our understanding of the reasons for their effectiveness remains limited. This work proposes a new way to understand self-attention networks: we show that their output can be decomposed into a sum of smaller terms, each involving the operation of a sequence of attention heads across layers. Using this decomposition, we prove that self-attention possesses a strong inductive bias towards "token uniformity". Specifically, without skip connections or multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), the output converges doubly exponentially to a rank-1 matrix. On the other hand, skip connections and MLPs stop the output from degeneration. Our experiments verify the identified convergence phenomena on different variants of standard transformer architectures.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Transformers for Dynamical Systems
papers.research_question: What are the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers for linear and nonlinear dynamical systems, and how do they relate to classical dynamical systems theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that softmax attention's convexity constraint limits representation of oscillatory linear dynamics, while for nonlinear systems with partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism enabling state reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The success of attention-based models in dynamical systems forecasting depends critically on the interplay between the system’s spectral properties, the observation regime, and the model’s architectural constraints.
papers.key_findings:
For linear systems, the convexity constraint of softmax attention restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings.
For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available.
Transformers can implicitly perform delay-coordinate embeddings, and the benefit of attention is most pronounced in partial observation regimes.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems and can lead to uniform averaging without them.
The latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding of the attractor.
papers.limitation:
Softmax normalization enforces non-negativity and convexity that restrict representable dynamics.
Positional encodings do not consistently benefit time-continuous physical systems.
Latent dimension must exceed the intrinsic manifold dimension to allow proper unfolding before projection.
Analysis is limited to single-layer Transformers, and deeper architectures may exhibit different behaviors.
future_direction: Multi-head attention and multi-layer architectures to understand how multiple heads might specialize in distinct modes.
Mechanistic interpretability for stiff and multiscale systems to see if attention offers advantages in adaptive integration.
Shared latent space geometry in foundation models to understand how distinct dynamical behaviors are embedded.
papers.abstract: Transformers are increasingly adopted for modeling and forecasting time-series, yet their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood from a dynamical systems perspective. In contrast to classical autoregressive and state-space models, which benefit from well-established theoretical foundations, Transformer architectures are typically treated as black boxes. This gap becomes particularly relevant as attention-based models are considered for general-purpose or zero-shot forecasting across diverse dynamical regimes. In this work, we do not propose a new forecasting model, but instead investigate the representational capabilities and limitations of single-layer Transformers when applied to dynamical data. Building on a dynamical systems perspective we interpret causal self-attention as a linear, history-dependent recurrence and analyze how it processes temporal information. Through a series of linear and nonlinear case studies, we identify distinct operational regimes. For linear systems, we show that the convexity constraint imposed by softmax attention fundamentally restricts the class of dynamics that can be represented, leading to oversmoothing in oscillatory settings. For nonlinear systems under partial observability, attention instead acts as an adaptive delay-embedding mechanism, enabling effective state reconstruction when sufficient temporal context and latent dimensionality are available. These results help bridge empirical observations with classical dynamical systems theory, providing insight into when and why Transformers succeed or fail as models of dynamical systems.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Higher Embedding Dimension Creates a Stronger World Model for a Simple Sorting Task
papers.research_question: How does embedding dimension affect the emergence of an internal world model in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps?
papers.core_contribution: Higher embedding dimensions lead to more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations (world models) in transformers trained on a sorting task, even after task accuracy saturates at lower dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build simple, structured internal world models even in constrained reinforcement learning settings, and increased model capacity (embedding dimension) improves the quality of these internal representations beyond what is reflected by task accuracy alone.
papers.key_findings:
The last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of input tokens.
The chosen adjacent swap corresponds to the largest difference between consecutive values in the encoded global ordering.
Task accuracy saturates at relatively low embedding dimensions (around 6 for length 6 sequences), but the fidelity and robustness of the internal ordering representation continue to improve up to around dimension 30.
Higher embedding dimensions make the learned internal mechanisms more consistent across different training runs and random seeds.
Low-dimension agents can fall into a 'local greedy trap', failing to form a coherent global ordering representation, a failure mode that decreases with higher embedding dimensions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited in scope and scale, focusing only on adjacent transposition sorting with 1-2 layer, single-head transformers, and does not explore more complex architectures or richer environments.
Computational budget restricted the ability to test broader ranges of sequence lengths or larger training runs.
future_direction: Relax the adjacency constraint to allow arbitrary in-place swaps to see if transformers discover known efficient algorithms or novel heuristics.
Introduce stochasticity into the environment (e.g., noisy token values or partial observability) to test if the ordering circuit emerges under uncertainty.
Explore hybrid training setups (e.g., supervised pre-training on optimal swaps followed by RL fine-tuning) to see if the ordering representation becomes more robust.
Introduce multi-head attention to examine if different heads specialize in complementary subproblems.
Test the robustness of the identified circuits under pruning or quantization, and apply similar analyses to structurally richer algorithmic tasks (e.g., graph algorithms).
papers.abstract: We investigate how embedding dimension affects the emergence of an internal "world model" in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps. Models achieve high accuracy even with very small embedding dimensions, but larger dimensions yield more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations. In particular, higher embedding dimensions strengthen the formation of structured internal representation and lead to better interpretability. After hundreds of experiments, we observe two consistent mechanisms: (1) the last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of tokens; and (2) the selected transposition aligns with the largest adjacent difference of these encoded values. Our results provide quantitative evidence that transformers build structured internal world models and that model size improves representation quality in addition to end performance. We release our metrics and analyses, which can be used to probe similar algorithmic tasks.

papers.title: Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
papers.research_question: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Specifically, is the structure given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process, and are belief states linearly represented in the residual stream?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical framework and empirical evidence that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the geometry of belief states (from the mixed-state presentation of the data-generating process) in their residual stream, even for complex fractal geometries, and that this representation captures information beyond local next-token predictions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers construct predictive representations that encode the complex geometry of belief updating over hidden states, capturing an inference process over the underlying structure of the data-generating process, which provides a concrete link between training data structure and internal model representations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on data from hidden Markov models (HMMs) linearly represent the belief state geometry of the mixed-state presentation in their residual stream, as verified by linear regression.
The belief state representation emerges during training and is not an artifact, as shown by controls including cross-validation and shuffling.
For processes where distinct belief states share the same next-token distribution (e.g., RRXOR), the belief state geometry is not well represented in the final layer alone but is distributed across multiple layers of the residual stream.
The representation captures information about the entire future distribution, not just the next token, as demonstrated by comparing pairwise distances between belief states versus next-token probabilities.
The belief state geometry is robust to the choice of using pre- or post-layer normalization activations.
papers.limitation:
Experimental validation focused on small-scale systems (HMMs with 3-5 states and vocabularies of 2-3 tokens), a significant simplification compared to modern language models.
For realistic systems, the dimensionality of the belief state simplex would exceed the residual stream dimension, suggesting representation must be compressed; the nature of this compression is not understood.
Explicitly computing ground-truth belief states becomes intractable as the size of the minimal generating structure and context window length grows, requiring new methodologies for validation in larger settings.
The work is limited to the stationary ergodic setting, though the framework is expected to extend to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes.
The paper establishes the representation of belief states but does not test whether transformers implement a circuit for performing Bayesian updates.
future_direction: Extending the framework to non-stationary and non-ergodic processes, such as in-context learning.
Understanding how belief state geometry is compressed when the simplex dimension exceeds the residual stream dimension.
Investigating the mapping between belief states and features, which is likely complex and architecture-dependent.
papers.abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation; the token identity then gets recreated at the top layer.
For MT, though representations get refined with context, less processing is happening and most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
Frequent tokens change more than rare ones in all layers for LM and MT, but for MLM the pattern is different with two stages; rare tokens generally influence more than frequent ones, except in MLM where the model learns not to over-rely on rare tokens before context is understood.
papers.limitation: Direct mutual information estimation from finite samples for densities on multi-dimensional spaces is challenging.
papers.abstract: We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: Learning, Memory, and the Role of Neural Network Architecture
papers.research_question: What tradeoffs exist between learning and memory processes in parallel versus layered neural network architectures during sequential tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Parallel networks produce accurate but specific representations that are hard to generalize, while layered networks produce coarse but easily adaptable representations, revealing tradeoffs between learning and memory due to differences in error landscape structure.
papers.conclusion: Different network architectures produce distinct error landscape structures, leading to tradeoffs in speed, accuracy, and adaptability, which is crucial for understanding and designing both natural and artificial learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Parallel (fan) networks achieve lower minimum error but higher maximum error compared to layered (stacked) networks.
Layered networks minimize average error and solution variance, leading to more generalizable representations.
Increasing network serialization (more layers) trades off accuracy for generalizability and reduces catastrophic failure.
Error landscape analysis shows fan networks have smooth landscapes with deep minima, while stacked networks have rough landscapes with multiple minima.
Under limited training time, layered networks are more consistent and less sensitive to temporal constraints than parallel networks.
papers.limitation: The study uses simplified feedforward networks without recurrent connections, temporal dynamics, or changes in intrinsic neuron properties, which may not fully capture biological complexity.
future_direction: Study the effects of dynamic structural changes like synapse formation and degradation on functional performance.
Incorporate recurrent connections to study oscillatory functions and signal propagation.
Examine the dependence of performance on the number of network connections and robustness to damage.
papers.abstract: The performance of information processing systems, from artificial neural networks to natural neuronal ensembles, depends heavily on the underlying system architecture. In this study, we compare the performance of parallel and layered network architectures during sequential tasks that require both acquisition and retention of information, thereby identifying tradeoffs between learning and memory processes. During the task of supervised, sequential function approximation, networks produce and adapt representations of external information. Performance is evaluated by statistically analyzing the error in these representations while varying the initial network state, the structure of the external information, and the time given to learn the information. We link performance to complexity in network architecture by characterizing local error landscape curvature. We find that variations in error landscape structure give rise to tradeoffs in performance; these include the ability of the network to maximize accuracy versus minimize inaccuracy and produce specific versus generalizable representations of information. Parallel networks generate smooth error landscapes with deep, narrow minima, enabling them to find highly specific representations given sufficient time. While accurate, however, these representations are difficult to generalize. In contrast, layered networks generate rough error landscapes with a variety of local minima, allowing them to quickly find coarse representations. Although less accurate, these representations are easily adaptable. The presence of measurable performance tradeoffs in both layered and parallel networks has implications for understanding the behavior of a wide variety of natural and artificial learning systems.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: How Does a Transformer Learn Compression? An Attention Study on Huffman and LZ4
papers.research_question: Can Transformers learn compression algorithms like Huffman and LZ4, and do their attention mechanisms provide interpretable insights into how they internalize these algorithms as finite state machines?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn compression algorithms, and their attention maps reveal how the encoder captures input statistics (state) and the decoder generates output bits, providing interpretability and evidence of their ability to understand finite state machines.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn compression algorithms, and their attention mechanisms provide interpretable insights into how they capture input state and generate output, suggesting their potential for understanding finite state machines.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy in learning Huffman and LZ4 compression algorithms.
Attention maps show the encoder's self-attention captures input context (e.g., previous symbols in Markov sources), forming a state.
Cross-attention maps clearly show the association between input symbols and output bits, indicating the decoder uses the encoder's state.
Ablation studies show that models without self-attention perform worse, highlighting its role in learning context.
For LZ4, attention maps show block-like patterns, indicating the model learns to associate input and output units.
papers.limitation: The encoder-only Transformer struggles with longer sequences for conditional Huffman encoding, potentially requiring larger models and more data.
papers.abstract: Transformers have excelled in natural language processing and vision domains. This leads to the intriguing proposition: can Transformers be adapted to a more generalized framework, such as understanding general finite state machines? To explore this, we trained a Transformer network on compression algorithms like Huffman and LZ4, viewing them as stepping stones towards mastering general finite state machines. Our analysis indicates that Transformers can adeptly internalize these methods and replicate essential states, echoing human-like interpretation via their attention mechanisms. This provides evidence of their capability to decipher practical finite state machines. Examining the attention maps offers insights into the Transformer’s methodology when engaging with these compression techniques. In Huffman encodings, the encoder predominantly focuses on input statistics to define the present state, which the decoder subsequently leverages to produce output bits. Remarkably, with a 2nd-order Markov input, the encoder’s attention is prominently directed at the previous two symbols, underscoring its proficiency in summarizing input statistics. The cross-attention maps further elucidate the exact association between input symbols and output bits. For the more complex LZ4 compression, the attention maps vividly portray the Transformer’s processing of input sequences and the close linkage between the input and resulting output bit stream. This study underscores the Transformer’s proficiency in comprehending compression algorithms and its keen ability to grasp input statistics, implying that its mechanisms, as illustrated by attention maps, provide profound interpretability.

papers.title: What are you sinking? A geometric approach on attention sink
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether attention sinks in transformers are architectural artifacts or manifestations of a fundamental geometric principle involving reference frames.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that attention sinks in transformers are not artifacts but geometric reference frames that establish coordinate systems in representational spaces.
papers.conclusion: The geometric perspective transforms understanding of transformer attention mechanisms and provides insights for architecture design and the relationship with attention sinks.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks are geometric reference frames that anchor representational spaces.
Three types of reference frames exist: centralized, distributed, and bidirectional, each associated with specific architectures.
Reference frames emerge early in training as optimal solutions to geometric constraints imposed by softmax.
Position encoding implementations significantly influence the type of reference frame that forms.
Removing attention sinks degrades model performance, indicating their essential role in maintaining geometric stability.
papers.abstract: Attention sink (AS) is a consistent pattern in transformer attention maps where certain tokens (often special tokens or positional anchors) disproportionately attract attention from other tokens. We show that in transformers, AS is not an architectural artifact, but it is the manifestation of a fundamental geometric principle: the establishment of reference frames that anchor representational spaces. We analyze several architectures and identify three distinct reference frame types, centralized, distributed, and bidirectional, that correlate with the attention sink phenomenon. We show that they emerge during the earliest stages of training as optimal solutions to the problem of establishing stable coordinate systems in high-dimensional spaces. We show the influence of architecture components, particularly position encoding implementations, on the specific type of reference frame. This perspective transforms our understanding of transformer attention mechanisms and provides insights for both architecture design and the relationship with AS.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: Traveling Words: A Geometric Interpretation of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can the internal mechanisms of transformers be understood from a geometric perspective, specifically the role of layer normalization and attention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric interpretation of transformers, showing how layer normalization projects features onto a hyper-sphere and how attention and feed-forward modules operate as geometric transformations on this sphere.
papers.conclusion: The geometric interpretation provides an intuitive understanding of transformers as processes that model the trajectory of word particles along the surface of a hyper-sphere, connecting and clarifying existing mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Layer normalization constrains d-dimensional input features to the surface of a (d-1) dimensional hyper-sphere.
Early attention heads show clear query-key patterns (e.g., repetition, precedence), while deeper layers exhibit more complex, subject-specific patterns.
The WV O matrix functions as a key-value store, and its singular value decomposition reveals interpretable, subject-specific singular vectors in deeper layers.
The geometric perspective unifies existing concepts like iterative refinement and contextual embeddings.
The word embedding matrix, when combined with layer normalization scale and bias, aligns common tokens with high-probability regions on the hyper-sphere.
papers.abstract: Transformers have significantly advanced the field of natural language processing, but comprehending their internal mechanisms remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel geometric perspective that elucidates the inner mechanisms of transformer operations. Our primary contribution is illustrating how layer normalization confines the latent features to a hyper-sphere, subsequently enabling attention to mold the semantic representation of words on this surface. This geometric viewpoint seamlessly connects established properties such as iterative refinement and contextual embeddings. We validate our insights by probing a pre-trained 124M parameter GPT-2 model. Our findings reveal clear query-key attention patterns in early layers and build upon prior observations regarding the subject-specific nature of attention heads at deeper layers. Harnessing these geometric insights, we present an intuitive understanding of transformers, depicting them as processes that model the trajectory of word particles along the hyper-sphere.

papers.title: Understanding Transformers through the Lens of Pavlovian Conditioning
papers.research_question: Why does the attention mechanism work so well? The paper investigates whether attention can be understood as implementing Pavlovian conditioning.
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a theoretical framework that reinterprets transformer attention as implementing Pavlovian conditioning, providing insights into memory capacity, error propagation, and potential architectural improvements inspired by neuroscience.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the success of attention may stem from implementing biological learning principles, and the theoretical framework provides a bridge between neuroscience and AI for building more interpretable and robust systems.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can store O(√dk) associations before interference degrades retrieval, as shown by a capacity theorem.
Error propagation in deep transformers scales as L·n^H/dk^H, revealing fundamental trade-offs between model depth, width, and head redundancy for reliability.
The framework suggests that biologically plausible learning rules (e.g., Delta rule, Oja's rule) could enhance transformer architectures by addressing stability and error correction.
Attention can be viewed as a dynamic associative memory that forms transient CS-US associations via a Hebbian rule during inference.
Stacking attention layers enables higher-order conditioning, providing a mechanistic account for in-context learning and compositional reasoning.
papers.limitation:
The framework finds its most direct mathematical parallel in linear attention, leaving a gap with the competitive dynamics of standard softmax attention.
The analysis focuses on attention-only architectures, omitting the role of MLP blocks which are critical in practice.
The model is a computational abstraction that simplifies the immense complexity of real biological neural circuits.
future_direction: Understanding the computational necessity of competitive normalization in softmax attention and its relation to biological mechanisms like lateral inhibition.
Investigating the role of MLP blocks within the conditioning framework, potentially as feature extractors or post-retrieval processors.
Understanding the interplay between slow gradient-based learning of projection matrices and fast inference-time association formation.
papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have revolutionized artificial intelligence (AI) through their attention mechanisms, yet the computational principles underlying their success remain opaque. We present a novel theoretical framework that reinterprets the core computation of attention as Pavlovian conditioning. Our model finds a direct mathematical analogue in linear attention, which simplifies the analysis of the underlying associative process. We demonstrate that attention's queries, keys, and values can be mapped to the three elements of classical conditioning: test stimuli that probe associations, conditional stimuli (CS) that serve as retrieval cues, and unconditional stimuli (US) that contain response information. Through this lens, we suggest that each attention operation constructs a transient associative memory via a Hebbian rule, where CS-US pairs form dynamic associations that test stimuli can later retrieve. Our framework yields several theoretical insights grounded in this linearized model: (1) a capacity theorem showing that attention heads can store O($\sqrt{d_k}$) associations before interference degrades retrieval; (2) an error propagation analysis revealing fundamental architectural trade-offs of balancing model depth, width, and head redundancy to maintain reliability; and (3) an understanding of how biologically plausible learning rules could enhance transformer architectures. By establishing this deep connection, we suggest that the success of modern AI may stem not from architectural novelty alone, but from implementing computational principles that biology optimized over millions of years of evolution.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Analyzing Transformer Dynamics as Movement through Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do the underlying mechanics of Transformer-based language models give rise to intelligent behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space, establishing a 'Theory of Transformers' where intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the model's composition functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework for understanding Transformers as movement through embedding space, explaining how intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the dynamics of encoding and decoding walks.
papers.key_findings:
Intelligent behaviors map to paths in Embedding Space which the Transformer random-walks through during inference.
LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths, assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors.
The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that its proximity to a token-vector reflects co-occurrence and conditioned probability.
Attention contributes a potentially redundant association-bias to the encoding walk, which aggregates features from the context via filtering and aggregation operations.
A three-way correspondence between similarity, association, and angular proximity is established in embedding space, leading to an associative organization.
papers.limitation: Experiments on concept space theory were limited to a single benchmark (Hellaswag) and a few models.
future_direction: Further investigation into the relative impact of vector similarity, position biases, filters, and decoding method across various model flavors.
papers.abstract: Transformer based language models exhibit intelligent behaviors such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, acquiring knowledge, reasoning, planning, reflecting and using tools. This paper explores how their underlying mechanics give rise to intelligent behaviors. Towards that end, we propose framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space. Examining Transformers through this perspective reveals key insights, establishing a Theory of Transformers: 1) Intelligent behaviours map to paths in Embedding Space which, the Transformer random-walks through during inferencing. 2) LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths. `Intelligence' is learnt by assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors. No learning can take place in-context; context only narrows the subset of paths sampled during decoding. 5) The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that it's proximity to a token-vector reflects its co-occurrence and conditioned probability. Thus, the physical arrangement of vectors in Embedding Space determines path probabilities. 6) Context vectors are composed by aggregating features of the sequence's tokens via a process we call the encoding walk. Attention contributes a - potentially redundant - association-bias to this process. 7) This process is comprised of two principal operation types: filtering (data independent) and aggregation (data dependent). This generalization unifies Transformers with other sequence models. Building upon this foundation, we formalize a popular semantic interpretation of embeddings into a ``concept-space theory'' and find some evidence of it's validity.

papers.title: Analyzing Transformers in Embedding Space
papers.research_question: Can Transformer parameters be interpreted in embedding space, and how can this be used for model alignment and transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for interpreting all Transformer parameters in embedding space and demonstrates applications in model alignment and zero-shot transfer.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can be understood in embedding space, enabling interpretation and transfer across models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer parameters can be interpreted in embedding space.
Models with shared vocabulary can be aligned in embedding space.
Knowledge can be transferred between models via embedding space without training.
papers.limitation:
The framework requires a linear language modeling head, which is not present in all architectures.
The choice of E' = E^T is empirical and may not be optimal.
future_direction: Extending the framework to handle non-linearities in the language modeling head.
Further exploration of the embedding space view for other architectures.
papers.abstract: Understanding Transformer-based models has attracted significant attention, as they lie at the heart of recent technological advances across machine learning. While most interpretability methods rely on running models over inputs, recent work has shown that a zero-pass approach, where parameters are interpreted directly without a forward/backward pass is feasible for some Transformer parameters, and for two-layer attention networks. In this work, we present a theoretical analysis where all parameters of a trained Transformer are interpreted by projecting them into the embedding space, that is, the space of vocabulary items they operate on. We derive a simple theoretical framework to support our arguments and provide ample evidence for its validity. First, an empirical analysis showing that parameters of both pretrained and fine-tuned models can be interpreted in embedding space. Second, we present two applications of our framework: (a) aligning the parameters of different models that share a vocabulary, and (b) constructing a classifier without training by “translating” the parameters of a fine-tuned classifier to parameters of a different model that was only pretrained. Overall, our findings open the door to interpretation methods that, at least in part, abstract away from model specifics and operate in the embedding space only.

papers.title: Understanding Transformer from the Perspective of Associative Memory
papers.research_question: How can Transformer architectures be understood from the perspective of associative memory, and what are the implications for memory capacity and update? Specifically, are Transformers fundamentally limited in expressivity, and can infinite context lead to infinite intelligence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a unified associative memory perspective on Transformers, analyzing memory capacity and update, and introduces DeltaFormer, which combines the high retrieval accuracy of Softmax Attention with the delta-rule update of DeltaNet to achieve higher expressivity.
papers.conclusion: Viewing Transformers through the prism of associative memory offers a unifying framework for understanding their memory capacity and update dynamics, and opens new avenues for architectural innovation.
papers.key_findings:
Softmax Attention with exponential kernel has higher memory capacity than linear attention, as shown by retrieval SNR analysis.
FFNs can be interpreted as associative memory with ReLU kernel, which encourages polysemanticity and allows superposition of knowledge.
DeltaFormer, which uses a delta-rule update, can track state exchanges and graph reachability more effectively than standard Transformers, demonstrating higher expressivity.
Theoretically, infinite context may lead to memory convergence, limiting in-context learning and posing challenges for unlimited context Transformers.
Curriculum learning and positional embeddings (like RoPE) affect optimization and length generalization in these models.
future_direction: Exploring kernel design for Attention and FFNs to balance retrieval precision and knowledge density.
Investigating multihead mechanisms in FFNs and gating mechanisms in attention.
Addressing the theoretical challenges of infinite context and memory convergence.
Pursuing the architectural endgame and optimal design for associative memory models.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we share our reflections and insights on understanding Transformer architectures through the lens of associative memory--a classic psychological concept inspired by human cognition. We start with the basics of associative memory (think simple linear attention) and then dive into two dimensions: Memory Capacity: How much can a Transformer really remember, and how well? We introduce retrieval SNR to measure this and use a kernel perspective to mathematically reveal why Softmax Attention is so effective. We also show how FFNs can be seen as a type of associative memory, leading to insights on their design and potential improvements. Memory Update: How do these memories learn and evolve? We present a unified framework for understanding how different Transformer variants (like DeltaNet and Softmax Attention) update their "knowledge base". This leads us to tackle two provocative questions: 1. Are Transformers fundamentally limited in what they can express, and can we break these barriers? 2. If a Transformer had infinite context, would it become infinitely intelligent? We want to demystify Transformer architecture, offering a clearer understanding of existing designs. This exploration aims to provide fresh insights and spark new avenues for Transformer innovation.

papers.title: From Cognition to Computation: A Comparative Review of Human Attention and Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between human attention and attention in Transformer architectures, and how can insights from human attention inform the development of more generalized artificial intelligence?
papers.core_contribution: This review provides a comparative analysis of human attention and Transformer attention mechanisms, identifying key similarities and differences, and proposes open research questions for integrating insights from human attention into AI.
papers.conclusion: The review compares human attention and Transformer attention, highlighting similarities and differences, and suggests that insights from human attention can guide the development of more generalized AI, while acknowledging the unique strengths of Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
Human attention and Transformer attention both involve selective attention, focusing on relevant information while filtering out irrelevant information.
Both human attention and Transformer attention involve contextual understanding, integrating context to interpret information.
Human attention has capacity constraints (limited working memory, sequential processing) while Transformers can process all inputs in parallel without such constraints.
Human attention involves top-down (goal-directed) and bottom-up (stimulus-driven) pathways, while Transformer attention is purely data-driven.
Human attention is intentional and tied to agency and social cognition, while Transformer attention is a mathematical construct without inherent cognitive states.
papers.limitation: The article is not an exhaustive review of either human attention or Transformer architecture, but a focused comparative analysis.
future_direction: Is emulating human capacity constraints beneficial?
How can models adopt a resource-rational approach from human attention?
How can attention modeling generate meaningful representations?
How can attention be formulated as an explicit component of agency?
papers.abstract: Attention is a cornerstone of human cognition that facilitates the efficient extraction of information in everyday life. Recent developments in artificial intelligence like the Transformer architecture also incorporate the idea of attention in model designs. However, despite the shared fundamental principle of selectively attending to information, human attention and the Transformer model display notable differences, particularly in their capacity constraints, attention pathways, and intentional mechanisms. Our review aims to provide a comparative analysis of these mechanisms from a cognitive-functional perspective, thereby shedding light on several open research questions. The exploration encourages interdisciplinary efforts to derive insights from human attention mechanisms in the pursuit of developing more generalized artificial intelligence.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Understanding the Staged Dynamics of Transformers in Learning Latent Structure
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn latent structure in a controlled setting, and what are the dynamics of this learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers learn latent structure in discrete stages, first acquiring coarse-grained rules before fine-grained details, and identifies a fundamental asymmetry where composition is robust but decomposition suffers with increasing complexity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn latent structure in a coarse-to-fine manner, and exhibit a fundamental asymmetry: they can robustly compose simple rules but struggle to decompose complex examples to discover underlying rules.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns latent structure in interpretable stages: first restricting predictions to the support set (in-support), then identifying the correct half of the structure, and finally pinpointing the exact target.
In composition tasks, the model robustly composes single-step rules to solve multi-step queries without performance degradation as sequence length increases.
In decomposition tasks, increasing the complexity (support hop length) delays learning, primarily by delaying the acquisition of the 'correct half' sub-skill.
An adjacency bias in the latent structure causes the model to learn the exact target before learning the correct half in the partial support task.
The learning dynamics are highly sensitive to hyperparameters; sub-optimal choices can prevent the model from converging or learning specific stages.
papers.limitation: Model performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameter configuration, and sub-optimal choices can prevent the model from learning some stages.
papers.abstract: While transformers can discover latent structure from context, the dynamics of how they acquire different components of the latent structure remain poorly understood. In this work, we use the Alchemy benchmark, to investigate the dynamics of latent structure learning. We train a small decoder-only transformer on three task variants: 1) inferring missing rules from partial contextual information, 2) composing simple rules to solve multi-step sequences, and 3) decomposing complex multi-step examples to infer intermediate steps. By factorizing each task into interpretable events, we show that the model acquires capabilities in discrete stages, first learning the coarse grained rules, before learning the complete latent structure. We also identify a crucial asymmetry, where the model can compose fundamental rules robustly, but struggles to decompose complex examples to discover the fundamental rules. These findings offer new insights into understanding how a transformer model learns latent structures, providing a granular view of how these capabilities evolve during training.

papers.title: How much do contextualized representations encode long-range context?
papers.research_question: How much do contextualized representations encode long-range context?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents an analysis of how much contextualized representations in autoregressive language models encode long-range context, using a perturbation setup and a new metric (ACCS). It finds that similar perplexity can mask differences in downstream performance, which is explained by varying degrees of long-range contextualization.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides representation-level insights into long-range context encoding, showing the benefits of hybrid architectures and larger model sizes, and suggests directions for improving long-context language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar perplexity can achieve markedly different downstream task performance, which correlates with the degree to which their hidden representations are contextualized by long-range content (measured by ACCS).
Models exhibit increasingly anisotropic representations as the input prefix becomes less compressible (i.e., has a higher compression rate).
Fully recurrent models (e.g., Mamba-2, mLSTM) and Transformers with ALiBi positional encoding rely primarily on local context for prediction.
RoPE-based Transformers can over-contextualize distant context, including noise, when tested on sequences longer than their pre-training length.
Hybrid models (e.g., Griffin, HybridMamba) more effectively contextualize the entire sequence structure, balancing local and global context without over-relying on either.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted over ten language models and could be extended to more recent architectures and open-access models.
The perturbation operation is constrained to simple token shuffling; other perturbations (e.g., maintaining n-gram statistics) could provide further insights.
Experiments on synthetic sequences were limited to the simplest possible regularity (periodic repetition).
The analysis primarily focused on base models with limited investigation on aligned models and no exploration on practical scenarios like reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Examining other more recent architectures and open-access models.
Investigating other perturbation operations beyond token shuffling.
Exploring other regularities in synthetic sequences to inspect model generalization.
papers.abstract: We analyze contextual representations in neural autoregressive language models, emphasizing long-range contexts that span several thousand tokens. Our methodology employs a perturbation setup and the metric \emph{Anisotropy-Calibrated Cosine Similarity}, to capture the degree of contextualization of long-range patterns from the perspective of representation geometry. We begin the analysis with a case study on standard decoder-only Transformers, demonstrating that similar perplexity can exhibit markedly different downstream task performance, which can be explained by the difference in contextualization of long-range content. Next, we extend the analysis to other models, covering recent novel architectural designs and various training configurations. The representation-level results illustrate a reduced capacity for high-complexity (i.e., less compressible) sequences across architectures, and that fully recurrent models rely heavily on local context, whereas hybrid models more effectively encode the entire sequence structure. Finally, preliminary analysis of model size and training configurations on the encoding of long-range context suggest potential directions for improving existing language models.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
